Maya, in her early thirties, short black hair in a pixie cut, a thin scar on her left eyebrow, wears a heather-grey sweater and a midnight-blue coat. In the early evening she sits down in the living room of her small apartment and reads a letter left near the lamp. The room is quiet, the curtains only half drawn, and the yellow light falls on the low table. Then she sets the letter on the table. So she stands up, still in the living room, and tidies the papers by the window. She glances toward the street, without leaving the room, and folds her arms for a moment. In the living room, she switches off the tall lamp and takes only the small envelope already opened.

The next day.
After that, in the kitchen, at 10 a.m., Maya opens the fridge. In the kitchen, she sets a cup on the counter. Then she pours hot water. She waits in a silence. She thinks of the beach. Suddenly Luca comes in, in his early forties, a short red beard, a bottle-green sweater, a beige canvas bag, a white paint stain on the sleeve. He leaves the bag by the door and looks for a second cup. He says, "We should go to the beach." Maya smiles at him, still in the kitchen, and closes the fridge. Then she hands him the cup. Luca takes a sip and sets the cup down. Maya puts the letter in a drawer, without leaving the room, and puts on her midnight-blue coat.

Later, at the station, Maya finds Luca by the departures board. The hall is noisy, the announcements follow one another, and a cold draught slides under the tall doors. They compare their tickets. Luca hands her a second envelope, thicker than the first. So Maya reads the name written on the back and slips it into her pocket. They stand for a moment under the clock, still at the station, without speaking. In a silence, Luca adjusts his bag. He says, "Nadia talked to me about Paris, but that is not for today."

At nightfall, in the café across the street, they sit down by the window. The room is narrow, the tables are dark wood, a radio plays very low. Maya opens the envelope. Then she takes out an old photograph and lays it flat. She looks Luca in his eyes and says nothing about the beach. In the café, the waiter brings two glasses of water. Suddenly Maya puts the photo away, still seated at the same table, and closes the envelope. Luca smiles and rests his hand near the glass, without standing up.

The next day.
At dawn, in Nadia's workshop, Maya pushes the door open. Nadia, in her late thirties, curly brown hair, round glasses, a yellow raincoat, black boots, a silver ring on her left hand, lifts a canvas against the wall. In the workshop, she switches on the lamp above the workbench. Then she holds out a rolled sketch to Maya. Luca arrives in turn and shuts the door. Nadia says, "I was thinking of the mountains, not of a harbour." Maya listens in a silence and unrolls the paper. She remembers Paris for a second only, then comes back to the drawing. So Nadia points to an ink mark, still in the workshop, and puts the brushes away. They talk a little longer, without leaving the room, and put on their coats.

After that, in the park, around noon, they walk along the path. The plane trees are almost bare, the gravel crunches, a dog passes in the distance. Maya stops near the kiosk. Then she rereads the sketch in the light. Luca sits on a bench, still in the park, and sets the bag at his feet. Nadia stays standing and checks the time. She says, "Only yesterday I was dreaming of the beach." Maya does not answer that and puts the paper away. In the park, a gust lifts the dead leaves. Suddenly they take the path again and walk as far as the gate.

Three days later.
On the harbour quay, at dusk, Maya, Luca and Nadia watch the boat move away. The water is dark, a bell rings somewhere, the air smells of salt and diesel. Then Maya takes the photograph from the pocket of her midnight-blue coat. So Luca steps closer, still on the quay, and reads the name on the back. Nadia pulls her yellow coat tighter. She thinks of the mountains, nothing more, and stays beside them. In a silence, Maya puts the photo away. They remain there until the boat is only a light, on the same quay, in the same dusk.
